pages.description: S.J.Res.88 would have ended the national emergency President Trump declared on April 2, 2025, to tax imports from nearly every country. Ending it would have canceled the resulting tariffs: a 10% tax on most imports, with higher rates on goods from certain countries.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.J.Res.88?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect If enacted on October 30, 2025, the bill would end the April 2 emergency and the extra taxes on imports based on it: “the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025, by the President in Executive Order 14257 (90 Fed. Reg. 15041) is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [1] Later tariff changes still rested on that order: “the terms of Executive Order 14257, as amended, shall continue to apply.” [2] Ending the emergency means “the corresponding tariffs could not be applied.” [3] This includes the emergency tax on the non-metal share of goods added to the metal tariff lists in August: “The non-steel and non-aluminum content will remain subject to the reciprocal and other applicable tariffs.” [4]

points.title: It lowers a cost barrier to replacing fossil fuels with less polluting power.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It lowers a cost barrier to replacing fossil fuels with less polluting power.

  • Because By September, the emergency's basic import tax had raised solar costs: “the baseline tariffs remained in effect and contributed to price increases across solar market segments” [5].
  • Because In April, before the higher China rate was suspended, an energy consultant ranked imported storage and grid equipment among the goods most exposed: “Grid-scale batteries and solar panels, as well as power transformers, are among the hardest hit by price increases on imports” [6].
  • Because CSIS warned in April that the taxes would also raise clean energy factory costs through imported inputs such as “cement, construction equipment” [7].
  • So Ending these extra taxes reduces a cost barrier both to installing clean power and to building factories that supply it.
  • Because Storage helps clean power replace fossil fuels: “Batteries allow renewables to replace fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal, while keeping a steady flow of power when sources like wind and solar are not producing.” [6]
  • Because Fossil fuel pollution harms plants and animals: “SO 2 causes acid rain, which is harmful to plants and to animals that live in water.” [8]
  • Because Burning fossil fuels also heats the planet: “Burning oil and gas emits greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide, which trap heat in the atmosphere and warm the planet” [9].
  • Because Warming damages habitats on land, in water and around ice. The U.N. climate science panel finds: “Climate change has caused substantial damages, and increasingly irreversible losses, in terrestrial, freshwater, cryospheric, and coastal and open ocean ecosystems (high confidence).” [10]
  • So Making that replacement easier supports [NAME]'s goal of protecting nature from air pollution and warming.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: By the bill date the higher China reciprocal rate was suspended through November 10, 2025. A 55% battery price estimate in the April AP article applied "if the tariffs are fully implemented on China." Sources: [11], [6].

Evidence note: An October 2025 Wood Mackenzie report calls generation step-up and power transformers the biggest bottlenecks, with delivery times measured in years, says transformer prices have stabilised, and describes tariffs as driving up costs and extending timelines. Sources: [12].

Evidence note: In the April AP article, experts said a trade slowdown might bring a brief and slight reduction in greenhouse gases, at most about 1% if full tariffs were implemented, and also said this would be outweighed by harm to clean energy. Sources: [6].

points.title: It removes obstacles to making and improving pollution cleanup equipment.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It removes obstacles to making and improving pollution cleanup equipment.

  • Because Denver manufacturer Geotech makes tools for cleaning contaminated water: “So we make a product to remediate or get oil, gas and diesel out of groundwater.” [13]
  • Because The company reports higher costs for imported parts: “It’s been reciprocal. So we're paying more for the components used to manufacture the product.” [13]
  • Because Managing changing tariffs also takes time away from better tools: “The time involved in managing the uncertainty is keeping us from focusing on creating innovative products for our customers and offering better service to our customers.” [13]
  • So Ending this emergency removes its taxes and rate changes from that work. Supporting the supply and improvement of tools that remove pollution gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Geotech owner names the aluminum and steel tariff as one expense, says it re-exports products, and said in August that the tariffs had become more predictable than in spring. Separate guidance says reciprocal duties are eligible for manufacturing drawback; the interview does not say whether Geotech claims it. Sources: [13], [14].

points.title: It eases the cost pressure on water treatment and reuse projects that protect rivers and habitats.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It eases the cost pressure on water treatment and reuse projects that protect rivers and habitats.

  • Because An April water-industry report said utilities import pumps, membranes and treatment supplies: “The tariffs will make importing these items more expensive for utilities.” [15]
  • Because Higher costs can delay treatment work. In May, when Chinese goods faced a 145% rate that was later suspended, Decatur, Arkansas, was postponing equipment purchases: “it will wait as long as possible for the rest, until the tariff issue is resolved” [16].
  • Because An April industry warning said water reuse projects also depend on equipment exposed to these taxes: “Membrane-based reuse and desalination systems—already under pressure in California, Texas, Florida—are particularly exposed.” [17]
  • Because Reuse treats polluted water: “This practice reduces pollutant discharges, such as nutrients, while increasing the reliability of community water supplies.” [18]
  • Because Reuse also supplies water for wildlife: “Water reuse can help restore ecosystems by providing them with a consistent water source.” [18]
  • So Removing these extra taxes from treatment equipment leaves more project money for cleaning water and sustaining habitats. Both serve [NAME]'s aim of protecting nature.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: By the bill date the higher China reciprocal rate was suspended through November 10, 2025. A 55% battery price estimate in the April AP article applied "if the tariffs are fully implemented on China." Sources: [11], [6].

Evidence note: An August 2025 report says Decatur had two ongoing projects to expand its wastewater plant's permitted capacity by December. It does not mention membranes or tariffs. Sources: [19].

points.title: It makes expanding recycling less costly.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It makes expanding recycling less costly.

  • Because Recycling relies on imported machinery: “Most of the sectors’ equipment comes from overseas, and high tariffs could hinder domestic recycling infrastructure buildout and rattle commodities markets.” [20]
  • Because The July industry report identified a tax on European recycling equipment: “Today they are subject to a 10 percent duty” [20].
  • Because The later EU tariff framework still included “a reciprocal tariff” [21].
  • Because Recycling protects nature: “Recycling benefits the environment by reducing the amount of waste sent to landfills and incinerators, conserving natural resources and preventing pollution.” [22]
  • So Ending the emergency tax on covered recycling machinery lowers a barrier to expanding this work. Conserving resources and preventing waste give [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: An October 2025 industry letter says recyclers import most shredder wear parts and that the expanded Section 232 metals program imposes a 50 percent duty on them. A BIS notice says non-metal content of derivative products stays subject to reciprocal tariffs. Sources: [23], [4].

points.title: It removes a U.S. source of tariff conflict that threatens Brazilian forests and savannas.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It removes a U.S. source of tariff conflict that threatens Brazilian forests and savannas.

  • Because China imposed an extra tax in response to the April policy: “in response to the United States' 34% IEEPA "reciprocal tariff" on imports from China, China announced an additional 34% tariff on all U.S. goods” [24].
  • Because That April retaliation still applied when Congress voted. USDA records an extension “for another 90 days from August 12, 2025, while retaining the 10 percent tariff” [25].
  • Because China's charge has moved with U.S.-China talks. After negotiations in Geneva, it “suspended 24 percent of the 34 percent” [25] charge.
  • Because The emergency also allows further U.S. tariff increases in response to retaliation: “Should any trading partner retaliate against the United States in response to this action through import duties on U.S. exports or other measures, I may further modify the HTSUS to increase or expand in scope the duties imposed under this order” [26].
  • Because After the May tariff reductions, Trase still identified a threat to Brazilian habitats: “there remains a risk that the surge in demand for Brazilian soy from China, resulting from the ongoing tensions, could increase deforestation and carbon emissions in Brazil.” [27]
  • So Ending the U.S. taxes behind that retaliation, and their escalation under this emergency, removes one source of a trade conflict that puts habitats at risk and makes a matching Chinese cut more plausible, though that remains China's choice. Protecting those habitats gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.
points.con_html:
Response Ending the U.S. emergency is not the Chinese tariff or buying decision needed to reduce demand for Brazilian soy. This response does not address the PRO's point about ending this emergency's power to escalate.

  • Because The bill's action concerns “the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025, by the President in Executive Order 14257” [1]. It does not change Chinese law.
  • Because The Chinese cut the PRO cites came through talks: “following a U.S.-China economic and trade negotiation in Geneva” [25]. A repeal by Congress would be one-sided, not a negotiated exchange.
  • Because Other Chinese charges would remain on U.S. farm goods: “certain U.S. agricultural products are also subject to Section 301 retaliatory tariffs” [25].
  • So The soy path needs China to lower its charge in response to a one-sided repeal. The PRO's negotiated example does not establish that response, so it does not establish less demand for Brazilian soy or less pressure to clear land.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: China's separate March 2025 farm duties (10-15 percent on 740 commodities) were in force on October 30, 2025 and were removed effective November 10 to implement a China-U.S. consensus. Section 301 and Section 232 retaliatory tariffs also applied to some U.S. farm goods. Sources: [25].

Evidence note: On February 26, 2026, after U.S. Customs stopped collecting IEEPA tariffs and began a Section 122 surcharge, China's commerce ministry said it would assess those measures and then decide whether to adjust its countermeasures targeting the original fentanyl-related and reciprocal tariffs. It also noted U.S. statements about tariffs through Section 301 and 232 investigations. This is an official position, not a final tariff adjustment. Because replacement tariffs applied, it is not a test of a one-sided repeal in October 2025. Sources: [28].

points.title: It takes away emergency tariff pressure aimed at weakening environmental rules.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It takes away emergency tariff pressure aimed at weakening environmental rules.

  • Because The September order tied tariff relief to “the scope and economic value of a trading partner’s commitments to the United States in its agreement on reciprocal trade” [29].
  • Because The EU tariff framework called for changes to companies' climate duties: “to propose changes to the requirement for a harmonised civil liability regime for due diligence failures and to climate-transition-related obligations.” [21]
  • Because In October, a further U.S. negotiating proposal “would commit Brussels to dropping rules requiring American firms to produce plans to fight climate change and end environmental and human rights violations in their supply chains.” [30] The same report says “the Commission does not intend to act on the criticism in the document” [30], so this example shows pressure applied, not a concession won.
  • So Ending the emergency takes away its import taxes as a lever for these demands. Defending rules against climate pollution and damage in supply chains serves [NAME]'s commitment to defend nature.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The European Commission proposed removing the EU-wide liability rule and changing the climate transition-plan duty on February 26, 2025, before the emergency. In October 2025, Politico reported that the Commission would not act on a further U.S. paper and would follow the August joint statement, which itself commits the EU to propose changes to those duties. This record does not show whether U.S. pressure affected the later legislation. Sources: [31], [30], [21].

points.title: It removes emergency tariff pressure for energy purchases that add climate pollution.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 It removes emergency tariff pressure for energy purchases that add climate pollution.

  • Because The EU tariff framework includes an energy purchase plan: “the European Union intends to procure US liquified natural gas, oil, and nuclear energy products” [21].
  • Because In August, a trade analyst explained the continuing tariff pressure: “The key to keeping the EU-US trade deal on track will be demonstrating rising EU energy purchases and investments in the US” [32].
  • Because The gas purchases have a pollution cost even when they replace pipeline gas. Chatham House researcher Chris Aylett explained: “Swapping pipeline gas for American LNG would further increase Europe's emissions” [9]. LNG means gas cooled into liquid for shipping.
  • Because The source explains why: “That's because LNG production and transport emits more methane — a greenhouse gas far more potent than CO2, though it doesn't stay as long in the atmosphere.” [9]
  • Because Human-caused climate change already causes “widespread adverse impacts and related losses and damages to nature and people” [10].
  • So Ending this emergency removes its tariff pressure to expand purchases with those pollution costs. Resisting that pressure gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill as a way to defend nature from climate harm.
points.con_html:
Response The energy pledge does not establish the extra switch from pipeline gas to U.S. shipped gas needed for the PRO's pollution claim.

  • Because LNG analyst Youri Leconte describes the deal as a continuation of an existing market shift: “This deal is more of a rebranding of positions that were already emerging due to the market shifts post-2022” [33].
  • Because The same report identifies who controls purchases: “Goldwyn said the commercial terms of any forthcoming contracts will still have to be competitive since the EU cannot compel European utilities to purchase US energy.” [33]
  • Because The PRO's emissions comparison concerns a particular replacement: “Swapping pipeline gas for American LNG would further increase Europe's emissions” [9]. LNG is gas cooled into liquid for shipping.
  • So The PRO needs to connect this emergency's pressure to purchases beyond those driven by existing markets, including a change from pipeline gas to shipped gas. The pledge and the pollution comparison do not establish that change, so they do not establish pollution this repeal would avoid.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The DW article reports an EU Commission spokesperson saying the deal would have no impact on EU decarbonization targets. CNBC reports analysts doubt the $750 billion pledge is feasible. S&P quotes an analyst calling it a very positive signal for U.S. LNG. Sources: [9], [32], [33].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose S.J.Res.88?
directions.main_effect_html:
Main effect If it took effect on October 30, 2025, the bill would end the April 2 emergency and the extra import taxes based on it: “the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025, by the President in Executive Order 14257 (90 Fed. Reg. 15041) is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [1] Ending that emergency means “the corresponding tariffs could not be applied.” [3]

  • Because The amended tariff rules kept extra taxes in place while trade deals were completed: “Goods of those trading partners will remain subject to the additional ad valorem duties provided in Annex I to this order until such time as those agreements are concluded, and I issue subsequent orders memorializing the terms of those agreements.” [2]
  • Because The September rules made tariff relief depend on “the scope and economic value of a trading partner’s commitments to the United States in its agreement on reciprocal trade” [29].
  • Because The deals offered relief from these taxes. Cambodia’s deal offered selected goods “a zero percent reciprocal tariff rate.” [34] Malaysia’s deal likewise promised that, for selected goods, “the United States shall not apply the additional ad valorem rate of duty applicable to those goods” [35].
  • Because Cambodia’s deal still awaited steps to take effect: “the United States and Cambodia will undertake domestic formalities in advance of the Agreement entering into force.” [34]
  • Because Its agreement allows action over broken commitments: “If either Party considers that the other Party has not complied with a provision of this Agreement, the Party may review the terms of the Agreement and take action in accordance with applicable domestic law.” [36]
  • So The bill would remove these extra taxes regardless of whether partners carried out their environmental promises. It would remove both an incentive to implement them and this emergency’s tariff tool for responding to breaches.

points.title: It removes tariff pressure for stronger protection against illegal logging.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It removes tariff pressure for stronger protection against illegal logging.

  • Because Cambodia promises action against illegal timber trade: “Cambodia shall take measures to combat, and cooperate with the United States to prevent, trade in illegally harvested forest products.” [37]
  • Because It also promises stronger enforcement: “Cambodia shall fully implement existing laws and regulations for forest sector governance, including anti-corruption measures, and strengthen institutions responsible for enforcing these laws.” [37]
  • Because Malaysia promises independent oversight of timber permits: “establish or uphold an independent forestry oversight body to supervise timber concessions and permits” [35].
  • So These promises support care for forests through checks on timber harvesting and stronger enforcement. Removing their tariff backing weakens an incentive for those protections, giving [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Section 301 separately lets USTR respond to trade agreement violations, generally after consulting the foreign country. In July 2025 USTR opened an investigation of Brazil that included illegal deforestation; no finding or penalty appears in this source. Sources: [38], [39].

Evidence note: Reasons 1-5 share one causal step: tariffs under this emergency as an incentive and enforcement tool. The Cambodia and Malaysia tariff schedules cap the rate at 19 percent and exempt listed goods, without product-level environmental conditions. The enforcement clause says a party may act "in accordance with applicable domestic law." Both agreements were awaiting entry into force on the bill date. Sources: [36], [35].

Brief context note: USTR's 2026 Trade Policy Agenda (March 2026) lists labor and environmental standards and national and economic security among ART commitments, and describes each ART as requiring the United States to maintain a modified tariff. It says the tools for maintaining those tariffs are subject to judicial review and may change, that it expects to keep working with partners to implement the deals, and that it will closely monitor implementation and enforce when necessary. It names Cambodia and Malaysia as signed ARTs and Thailand as a framework deal. This is official U.S. intention from after the bill date, when replacement tariffs applied. It reports no foreign compliance and no labor or environmental result, and it does not test a hypothetical repeal on October 30, 2025. Sources: [40].

Brief context note: On February 21, 2026, Malaysia's trade ministry said Malaysia had signed the ART but not ratified it and was assessing recent U.S. legal and policy developments. The statement recognized that the United States retains other legal mechanisms to impose tariffs and noted a temporary 10% tariff. It reports no withdrawal, termination or implementation result. This replacement-tariff setting differs from the frozen comparison of ending the emergency on October 30, 2025. Sources: [41].

points.title: It removes tariff pressure to protect wild animals and plants from illegal trade.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It removes tariff pressure to protect wild animals and plants from illegal trade.

  • Because Cambodia promises action against “the trade of wild fauna and flora that, based on credible evidence, were taken or traded in violation of its law or another applicable law” [37].
  • Because Its promised actions include “take measures to dismantle organized trafficking networks involved in nature crimes.” [37]
  • Because Malaysia promises stronger enforcement of international rules on trade in endangered species, known as CITES: “Malaysia shall strengthen implementation of CITES to ensure legal and sustainable trade of CITES-listed species, including compliance with CITES reporting requirements for species listed in Appendix I of CITES, such as pangolins.” [35]
  • So [NAME]’s care for wild animals and plants supports these protections. The bill removes a tariff incentive for carrying them out.

Point 3 It removes tariff pressure to curb overfishing and protect marine wildlife.

  • Because Cambodia promises to ensure “its fisheries subsidies do not contribute to overcapacity and overfishing” [37]—so government payments do not support fleets that catch too much fish.
  • Because Its fishing management system must promote conservation: “promotes the long-term conservation of marine species including sharks, sea turtles, seabirds, and marine mammals.” [37]
  • Because Cambodia also promises stronger enforcement to “effectively combat illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing and deter trade in products from IUU fishing” [37].
  • So These promises protect fish stocks and marine animals. Removing their tariff backing weakens pressure for those protections, which [NAME] has a reason to preserve.

points.pro_html:
Point 4 It removes tariff pressure to use materials carefully and recover them from waste.

  • Because Cambodia promises steps toward less wasteful use of resources: “Cambodia shall take measures to promote more resource efficient economies.” [37]
  • Because The deal names better product design as one way to do that: “encouraging innovation that promotes circularity, for example through improving resource efficiency in product design” [37].
  • Because Malaysia promises to recover minerals from waste: “Malaysia shall take measures to promote the recovery of critical minerals from domestic waste streams.” [35] The agreement identifies “the collection of electronic waste and spent lithium-ion batteries for recycling and recovering critical minerals” [35] as one way to do this.
  • So [NAME]’s care for nature supports using natural resources carefully and recovering materials from discarded goods. The bill removes a tariff incentive for those steps.

Point 5 It removes tariff pressure for a process people can use to defend nature.

  • Because Cambodia’s promised rules for its central government require public input: “conduct public consultations for proposed regulatory actions in a transparent manner; allow adequate time for interested persons, domestic and foreign, to submit comments, taking into account the complexity or possible impact of the proposed regulation; and give consideration to comments received” [37].
  • So Applied to environmental rules, this process gives people a way to argue for nature’s protection and requires the government to consider their comments.
  • So Taking part in defending nature matters to [NAME]. Removing a tariff incentive for this public involvement gives [NAME] another reason to oppose the bill.

points.title: It removes a price restraint on clothing purchases and the environmental harm tied to them.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It removes a price restraint on clothing purchases and the environmental harm tied to them.

  • Because Bangladesh’s garment manufacturers’ association vice president reported a drop in clothing demand after the new reciprocal tax: “US consumer spending has slowed due to the high tariff. Clothing consumption is declining, and buyers are not placing new orders because of it.” [44]
  • Because Clothing producers reported fewer orders because of the reciprocal tax itself. Bangladesh’s knitwear producers’ association president said: “Due to the reciprocal tariff, US buyers are delaying or reducing orders as they negotiate to shift part of the tariff burden onto Bangladeshi suppliers.” [44]
  • So Ending this extra import cost removes a restraint on orders for new clothing.
  • Because Making short-lived clothing and throwing it away harms nature. UNEP explains: “These clothes are often worn for only a short time, then jettisoned into landfills or incinerated. This feeds climate change, depletes natural resources and floods land, sea and air with hazardous chemicals.” [45]
  • Because Clothing also puts pressure on scarce water. UNEP finds that “natural fibre production (cotton cultivation) and the consumer use phase stand out as particularly important with respect to the water scarcity impact.” [46]
  • Because Cutting the freight needed for new purchases is also a route to less pollution. Opportunity Green explains that “even small savings in weight and transport time can add up into big reductions in emissions.” [47]
  • So The bill gives up a price check on new clothing and its demand for production, materials, water, transport, and waste disposal. [NAME]’s wish to protect nature from destruction and pollution gives a reason to oppose losing that restraint.

pages.bill_title: a joint resolution terminating the national emergency declared to impose global tariffs
statements: that the weak and vulnerable in society be protected
that every person in the world have equal opportunities in life
that everyone be treated justly, even people they don't know
pages.description: S.J.Res.88 would have ended the national emergency President Trump declared on April 2, 2025, to tax imports from nearly every country. Ending it would have canceled the resulting tariffs: a 10% tax on most imports, with higher rates on goods from certain countries.
pages.comparison: If this bill took effect on October 30, 2025, versus law in force then

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.J.Res.88?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect If enacted on October 30, 2025, S.J.Res.88 would end the April 2 emergency and the extra import taxes based on it, at the rates then in force. The emergency “is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution” [1]. The July order changing the rates still acts “to deal with the national emergency declared in Executive Order 14257” [2]. Ending that emergency means “the corresponding tariffs could not be applied” [3].

points.title: Removing these taxes helps poorer families afford basic needs and eases an unequal burden.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Removing these taxes helps poorer families afford basic needs and eases an unequal burden.

  • Because The taxes raise shoppers' costs. An October study of the reciprocal taxes on Bangladeshi clothing explains: “The more likely outcome is that U.S. importers, retailers, and consumers will shoulder much of the additional cost.” [4]
  • Because Poorer households spend more of their income buying goods and services. Yale explains that “lower-income households spend a larger fraction of their income than higher-income households do, on average” [5].
  • Because People already buying the cheapest necessities have little room to cut costs. Marketplace explains: “If you’re already buying your underwear from the most affordable brands, there’s nothing cheaper to switch to.” [6] It describes the food risk: “Because healthier food tends to be more expensive, and if you can’t afford the cheapest vegetables, then you don’t buy any.” [6]
  • So Ending these taxes removes pressure on the price of necessities, protecting food and clothing budgets where money is tightest. Protecting those least able to pay serves [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people and fair treatment.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: An April 2025 Marketplace article says prices of some goods may not fall back after tariffs are removed if demand stays high or firms rebuild supply chains, while prices of goods like fruit and vegetables may be less sticky and prices likely decline if demand had fallen. Sources: [7].

points.title: Easing costs gives small business owners a fairer chance to keep their livelihoods and the jobs they support.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Easing costs gives small business owners a fairer chance to keep their livelihoods and the jobs they support.

  • Because The Chamber of Commerce reports: “Small businesses, manufacturers, and ranchers are struggling with higher costs” [8].
  • Because Small firms have fewer ways to handle tariff costs than larger rivals. CNBC explains: “Their margins are slimmer, their supply chains less diverse and their negotiating power with vendors dampened by the smaller sizes of their orders.” [9]
  • Because These costs can take money away from jobs. At Reekon Tools, “The hundreds of thousands of dollars Reed planned to use to hire between three and five designers and engineers is now going to tariffs instead, he said.” [9]
  • So Ending the emergency's taxes frees money that affected firms need to operate and hire. It removes a burden that people running smaller firms are less able to absorb. That supports fair opportunities to earn a living for owners and workers.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: CNBC reports Reekon's total expected 2025 tariffs at more than $400,000, without splitting them by program. The same report says Reed had held most prices and that sales of a new tool fell short of projections. Sources: [9].

points.title: Ending this source of sudden tax changes protects access to jobs and safe work.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Ending this source of sudden tax changes protects access to jobs and safe work.

  • Because The order allows further tax rises, including power to “increase duties under this order” [10].
  • Because Uncertainty about tariff rates holds back staffing. In its June 2025 survey of firms in the Fourth Federal Reserve District, the Cleveland Fed found that “19 percent of contacts said that tariff-related uncertainty had led their firm to scale back staffing plans” [11].
  • Because Uncertainty also threatens workers' protection abroad. Asked about tariff uncertainty, the ILO's Sara Park explained: “During periods of crisis or uncertainty, investment generally pauses. One concern is that factories stop investing in improving working conditions, which could affect occupational safety and health.” [12]
  • So Ending the emergency removes its power to make these tax rates change again. That removes a source of pressure to hold back hiring and safety improvements. Protecting opportunities to find paid work and stay safe at work serves [NAME]'s concern for workers, including vulnerable workers abroad.
points.con_html:
Response Closing one route for sudden tax changes does not establish less uncertainty about the rates firms would actually pay. This response does not deny that the bill ends this order's own power to raise rates.

  • Because Replacement plans were announced before the vote. In a May interview transcribed in a June 2 court filing, trade adviser Peter Navarro said: “So you can assume that even if we lose we will do it another way.” [13] This was a stated plan to keep the tariff policy after losing its emergency-law basis.
  • Because An October analysis described a proposed bridge to other tariff powers: “Five months of Section 122 tariffs would provide time for the Commerce Department to do the investigation required by Section 232 of the Trade Act of 1962 for a president to impose tariffs for national security reasons.” [14] Section 122’s use would still have to meet that law’s conditions.
  • So Hiring and safety plans respond to uncertainty about future rates, whichever law sets them. Given the announced search for replacement powers, the PRO's evidence does not establish that ending this legal route would make rates more predictable.

points.title: Removing a proven trigger for retaliation reduces a threat to farm families and others who depend on exports.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Removing a proven trigger for retaliation reduces a threat to farm families and others who depend on exports.

  • Because China directly answered the April taxes with taxes on U.S. exports. CRS reports that “in response to the United States' 34% IEEPA "reciprocal tariff" on imports from China, China announced an additional 34% tariff on all U.S. goods” [15].
  • Because Retaliation puts sellers at a disadvantage: “Foreign retaliatory tariffs on U.S. exports make U.S. goods less competitive in foreign markets compared to goods not subject to tariffs” [15]. October reporting shows the stakes for farm livelihoods: one Minnesota grower was selling soybeans “for less than what it cost to produce them.” [16]
  • Because Reducing the U.S. taxes has already helped ease this conflict. The May joint agreement paired U.S. tariff cuts with China's commitment to “suspend or remove the non-tariff countermeasures taken against the United States since April 2, 2025.” [17]
  • So Ending this tariff trigger and its power to fuel new rounds of retaliation reduces an avoidable risk to export sales. Protecting people whose livelihoods are caught in that conflict gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: China's March farm duties responded to a U.S. action separate from the April emergency. On October 30, 2025, China said the U.S. would suspend the 24 percent reciprocal tariff for another year and that China would adjust its countermeasures, and reported consensus on expanding agricultural trade. The May deal left China's 10 percent charge in place. Sources: [15], [18], [17].

Evidence note: On February 26, 2026, after U.S. Customs stopped collecting IEEPA tariffs and began a Section 122 surcharge, China's commerce ministry said it would assess those measures and then decide whether to adjust its countermeasures targeting the original fentanyl-related and reciprocal tariffs. It also noted U.S. statements about tariffs through Section 301 and 232 investigations. This is an official position, not a final tariff adjustment. Because replacement tariffs applied, it is not a test of a one-sided repeal in October 2025. Sources: [19].

points.title: Removing barriers to poor countries' exports protects workers' basic needs and their families' future chances.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Removing barriers to poor countries' exports protects workers' basic needs and their families' future chances.

  • Because The reciprocal taxes threaten demand for these workers' goods. The October clothing study warns that “the elevated tariffs are set to reduce demand, squeeze suppliers, and depress investment in future capacity” [4].
  • Because This reaches an important source of women's earnings. UN Trade and Development's October 30 report states: “The textile and apparel industry, an important source of employment for women in many LDCs, has been hit hardest.” [20] LDCs are countries the UN classifies as least developed.
  • Because Workers can have few other ways to earn a living. The Fuller Project reports: “Women in Lesotho, Bangladesh and Cambodia all said there were no realistic employment alternatives available to them.” [21] A worker-rights researcher warns that if these jobs go, “workers will struggle to pay for basic necessities such as food, school fees, and healthcare” [21].
  • Because Lost sales and investment also threaten future opportunities. The UN report warns: “Higher levels of US protection on manufacturing, agriculture and food risk dampening LDCs’ hard-won progress in building productive capacities, reducing commodity dependence and promoting value addition.” [20] That means building the ability to make more goods, sell a wider range of products and do more of the work that adds to their value.
  • So Removing the added tax supports demand for workers' goods and investment in future production. That protects earnings for food, schooling and healthcare, women's ability to earn, and poorer countries' routes to better work. These are reasons for [NAME], who values protection and equal life chances for people worldwide.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: UNCTAD says reciprocal and sectoral tariffs and expiring preference programs together raised tariffs on LDCs. The Bangladesh brief says suppliers with smaller add-ons may gain orders at least temporarily. Sources: [20], [4].

points.title: Ending these taxes lifts a disproportionate burden from people in small, poor economies.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 Ending these taxes lifts a disproportionate burden from people in small, poor economies.

  • Because The emergency's stated problem is reflected in “large and persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficits” [10]—the United States buying more goods abroad than it sells abroad.
  • Because Small, poor economies have little ability to buy U.S. goods. The UN explains: “As many of these economies are small in size, structurally weak with low purchasing power, they offer limited export market opportunities for the US.” [22]
  • Because Lesotho shows the mismatch. Its share of the U.S. goods trade deficit in the UN's 2024 data was tiny: “Lesotho 0.019%” [23]. It still faced an added tax under the later rates; September reporting describes “a much-reduced tariff of 15%” [21].
  • So Ending the reciprocal taxes removes a charge on people whose countries have little ability to buy U.S. goods and contribute little to the stated problem. Fair treatment calls for burdens to reflect people's circumstances and their part in the problem. Sparing poor people this disproportionate burden serves [NAME]'s concern for justice across borders.
points.con_html:
Response The deficit-share comparison does not establish the unfair treatment it is used to prove.

  • Because The UN’s “Lesotho 0.019%” [23] measures a country’s share of the total U.S. goods trade deficit. The reported “much-reduced tariff of 15%” [21] measures a tax on the value of covered imports. Neither percentage measures the tax cost relative to a poor person’s income.
  • Because The PRO adds a rule that the burden is unjust because the country contributes little to the total deficit. [NAME]’s concern for just treatment of people does not by itself establish that national trade shares determine the burdens individuals should bear.
  • So A small country’s small share of a large country’s deficit is not a measure of injustice to its workers. The two percentages do not substantiate the claimed disproportionate burden or show that ending it would correct unjust treatment.

points.title: Ending this use of emergency power checks burdens imposed without the usual required investigation.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 Ending this use of emergency power checks burdens imposed without the usual required investigation.

  • Because The emergency-powers law skips a check found in other main tariff laws. CRS explains that it “does not require any agency to conduct an investigation or make findings of fact before the President acts.” [24]
  • Because Scrutiny helps protect people who bear the costs. The Chamber calls for “appropriate stakeholder consultation and a methodical assessment of costs” [8] before raising taxes on traded goods.
  • Because This bill makes Congress's power to end that use of emergency authority effective. CRS explains that Congress may end “a national emergency—and any authorities the President exercises thereunder—by enacting into law a joint resolution of disapproval.” [24]
  • So People whose food budgets and jobs are at stake deserve public scrutiny of burdens placed on them. Ending this emergency enforces Congress's check on a route that skips required investigation. That supports [NAME]'s concern that everyone be treated justly.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Executive Order 14257 says the President received final results of investigations ordered by earlier memoranda on April 1, 2025. CRS says IEEPA does not require any agency to investigate or make findings. The Chamber letter says a more deliberative process could ensure consultation and lists S.J.Res.88 among responsive proposals. Sources: [10], [24], [8].

directions.main_effect_html:
Main effect If enacted on October 30, 2025, the resolution would end the April 2 tariff emergency: “the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025, by the President in Executive Order 14257 (90 Fed. Reg. 15041) is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [1] Its import taxes could no longer be used: “Doing so would mean that the corresponding tariffs could not be applied.” [3]

  • Because Cutting these taxes is a bargaining tool. The September 5 order makes tax cuts depend on “the scope and economic value of a trading partner’s commitments to the United States in its agreement on reciprocal trade” [25].
  • Because Malaysia’s signed October 26 deal uses this emergency’s taxes. The United States agreed to “maintain at 19 percent the reciprocal tariffs first set forth in Executive Order 14257 of April 2, 2025, as amended” [26] and identified goods “to receive a zero percent reciprocal tariff rate.” [26]
  • So Ending the emergency removes both price protection for covered U.S. goods and the option to offer cuts in these taxes in return for other governments’ actions.

points.title: It removes price protection from factory work that offers opportunities to people with limited job options.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It removes price protection from factory work that offers opportunities to people with limited job options.

  • Because Unionwear’s president explains the price protection: “Each tariff increase reduces the cost advantage of imports, making our domestic production more competitive without us having to change anything.” [27] He also explains why taxes on the firm’s supplies do little to offset that benefit: “We source our raw materials domestically when possible, so tariffs on finished goods help us while tariffs on materials have minimal impact on our cost structure.” [27]
  • Because Domestic makers have reported winning work. Royal Apparel said: “Several production programs that were initially set to go overseas have now been redirected to Royal Apparel” [28].
  • Because This demand reaches employers that open doors to people with disabilities. Stakes Manufacturing’s cofounder said its April garment partnership would “meet the rising demand driven by recent tariff changes” [28]. Reporting on the firm found: “10% of the 225 employees at Stakes Manufacturing are people with an intellectual or developmental disability.” [29]
  • Because Earlier China-trade import shocks, which do not measure the effect of this change, show how hard lost factory work can be to replace for people without degrees: “Almost all of the manufacturing job losses affected workers without a college degree, and this group saw almost no job gains in the next two decades.” [30]
  • Because Those earlier import shocks also harmed children through their parents’ lost earnings. A study of trade shocks to young men’s relative earnings found that “these shocks heighten male idleness and premature mortality, and raise the share of mothers who are unwed and the share of children living in below-poverty, single-headed households.” [31]
  • So Removing this price protection puts vulnerable workers’ opportunities and their families’ security at risk. Protecting people who face barriers to work, and children who bear the costs of lost work, gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Executive Order 14257 duties are added to other duties that the bill leaves in place. The redirected orders concern Royal Apparel and the disability-employment figure concerns Stakes; the Stakes statement refers to recent tariff changes generally. The Autor, Dorn and Hanson study period is 1990-2014. Sources: [10], [28], [29], [31].

Evidence note: Autor, Beck, Dorn and Hanson report that the 2018-2019 import tariffs did not appear to increase manufacturing employment. Flaaen and Pierce report that U.S. manufacturing industries more exposed to tariff increases had relative employment reductions, with a positive protection effect offset by input costs and retaliation. Both studies concern earlier tariffs. Sources: [32], [33].

points.pro_html:
Point 2 It removes a way to press governments to stop treating people’s work unfairly because it comes from abroad.

  • Because The signed Cambodia deal promises equal access for farm goods: “Cambodia shall provide non-discriminatory market access for U.S. agricultural goods as set forth in this Agreement.” [36]
  • Because It also protects people selling services against worse treatment than local or other foreign suppliers: “Cambodia shall refrain from imposing new barriers that provide less favorable treatment to U.S. services suppliers than the treatment afforded to domestic services suppliers and services suppliers from any third country, jurisdiction, or economy.” [36]
  • Because More talks to remove barriers were underway: “President Trump remains in active negotiations with many countries to further eliminate barriers to U.S. exports.” [37]
  • So The bill removes these U.S. import taxes without requiring governments to agree to or carry out such changes. That removes an incentive to end discrimination that limits people’s chances to earn a living. Equal opportunities and just treatment give [NAME] a reason to oppose.

pages.description: S.J.Res.88 would have ended the national emergency President Trump declared on April 2, 2025, to tax imports from nearly every country. Ending it would have canceled the resulting tariffs: a 10% tax on most imports, with higher rates on goods from certain countries.
pages.comparison: If this bill took effect on October 30, 2025, versus law in force then

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.J.Res.88?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Had it taken effect on October 30, 2025, the bill would have ended the April 2 emergency and the added import taxes imposed under it. The bill says the emergency “is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [1] Analysis of ending that same emergency explains: “Doing so would mean that the corresponding tariffs could not be applied.” [2]

points.title: It removes a country-based barrier to doing business with people despite disagreements with their governments.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It removes a country-based barrier to doing business with people despite disagreements with their governments.

  • Because The program applies across countries, rather than testing each seller’s views: “all imports from all trading partners except as otherwise provided herein.” [3]
  • Because The April order makes agreement with U.S. policy one condition for lowering these taxes: “Should any trading partner take significant steps to remedy non-reciprocal trade arrangements and align sufficiently with the United States on economic and national security matters, I may further modify the HTSUS to decrease or limit in scope the duties imposed under this order.” [3]
  • Because The July revision again counted government alignment when setting rates, saying some partners “have failed to align sufficiently with the United States on economic and national-security matters.” [4]
  • So A willing seller and buyer face this added barrier because of the goods’ country of origin, regardless of the seller’s own views. Ending it removes that penalty from their business ties, including ties across governments’ disagreements.
  • Because Keeping willing relationships open without requiring agreement with people’s governments is one way to act on acceptance across national and political differences.
  • So [NAME]’s tolerance gives a reason to remove this barrier to accepting foreign people as business partners.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO leaves a gap between removing a cost on foreign goods and accepting foreign people across disagreements.

  • Because The taxes follow the product’s origin. Shipping guidance explains: “The tariffs are applied based upon the product’s country of origin rather than the country from which the product was shipped.” [5]
  • Because The condition for lowering rates concerns governments’ actions: “Should any trading partner take significant steps to remedy non-reciprocal trade arrangements and align sufficiently with the United States on economic and national security matters, I may further modify the HTSUS to decrease or limit in scope the duties imposed under this order.” [3]
  • Because Where goods come from, what a government does, and whether people accept one another are different things. A product’s origin does not establish its seller’s nationality or views. A trade cost can apply within a relationship in which people already accept one another across differences.
  • So Removing this charge changes the terms of trade. The PRO still needs to explain why easing those terms puts acceptance of different people into practice. The government-alignment condition does not supply that link.

points.title: It helps people keep their food traditions and the shared places where others can learn about them.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It helps people keep their food traditions and the shared places where others can learn about them.

  • Because The costs were still reaching cultural grocers in October. At Chicago’s 88 Marketplace, the manager said “the recent 15% import tariffs on South Korean products will make it harder for the grocer to keep prices down.” [6]
  • Because Customers were already paying some of those costs: “While the store is absorbing some of the price increases, Zhu said it has still been forced to pass along some cost hikes to customers.” [6]
  • Because Local replacements are hard to find: “And often, these items, like grains, spices or herbs, are not easily sourced in the U.S.” [6]
  • Because These foods support cultural practices: “Food is an important way Asian Americans take part in their culture.” [7]
  • So Ending this added tax removes a cost that makes familiar foods harder to stock and afford. Helping neighbors keep their own food traditions puts acceptance of different ways of life into practice.
  • Because The grocers also provide places for people from different backgrounds to meet. Reporting on Chicago’s Gangnam Market explains: “The store hosts different activities, including mahjong games, K-pop dance performances and anime exhibitions, for all ages and backgrounds.” [8]
  • So The same relief helps sustain shared spaces for meeting people and learning about their cultures. [NAME]’s wish to listen to and understand different people gives a further reason to protect these opportunities.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: In the October Sun-Times report, the 88 Marketplace manager says tariffs were not as high as in April and May and describes supply shortages. A December Medill report says inflation and tariffs together threaten these supermarkets. Sources: [6], [8].

points.title: It removes part of a trade conflict that puts Asian Americans at risk of blame for another country’s actions.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It removes part of a trade conflict that puts Asian Americans at risk of blame for another country’s actions.

  • Because This program allows higher taxes in response to another country’s retaliation: “Should any trading partner retaliate against the United States in response to this action through import duties on U.S. exports or other measures, I may further modify the HTSUS to increase or expand in scope the duties imposed under this order to ensure the efficacy of this action.” [3]
  • Because Karen Umemoto, director of UCLA’s Asian American Studies Center, explains how conflict with a country can become hostility toward people: “When a top political leader blames another country for its woes, Americans often scapegoat those around them who ‘look like the enemy.’” [9]
  • Because She identifies renewed resentment in the 2025 tariff conflict: “And with the tariff war, we sense resentment rising again.” [9]
  • So Ending this tariff program and its power to raise taxes in retaliation removes one source of the conflict behind that warning. [NAME] has reason to remove a policy that feeds the risk of treating Asian Americans as enemies because of their ancestry.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The New Republic article is an opinion piece. It says tariffs may not be intuitively xenophobic and places them within a wider set of policies and rhetoric, including deportation. Umemoto describes scapegoating following a leader's blame and says "we sense resentment rising." Sources: [9].

  • Because Malaysia's October 26 trade deal uses the tariffs the bill would end: “the reciprocal tariffs first set forth in Executive Order 14257 of April 2, 2025, as amended” [10].
  • Because The September 5 order ties tariff relief to partners' promises. The factors governing relief include “the scope and economic value of a trading partner’s commitments to the United States in its agreement on reciprocal trade” [11].
  • Because Malaysia's agreement allows action over broken promises: “If a Party considers that the other Party has not complied with a provision of this Agreement, the Party may review the terms of this Agreement and take action in accordance with applicable domestic law.” [12]
  • Because The U.S. trade representative described tariffs as a way to enforce trade deals: “If they don't honor their agreements with the U.S., then "the president has his tariff authority," Greer said.” [13] The same report quotes him saying the deals are “going to stick regardless of what happens in litigation” [13], which it questions.

  • Because The declaration includes “the elimination of discrimination in respect of employment and occupation” [15].
  • Because The ILO's discrimination standard names “race, colour, sex, religion, political opinion, national extraction or social origin” [16].

Point 8 It removes tariff pressure supporting dialogue and mutual respect between Thailand and Cambodia.

  • Because The connection continued at the October 26 signing. Trump said: “We do transactions, lots of them, with both nations as long as they live in peace” [31].

pages.description: S.J.Res.88 would have ended the national emergency President Trump declared on April 2, 2025, to tax imports from nearly every country. Ending it would have canceled the resulting tariffs: a 10% tax on most imports, with higher rates on goods from certain countries.
pages.comparison: If this bill took effect on October 30, 2025, versus law in force then

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.J.Res.88?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect If enacted on October 30, 2025, the bill would end the April 2 tariff emergency: “is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [1] Ending that emergency ends the added import taxes based on it: “Doing so would mean that the corresponding tariffs could not be applied.” [2] These reasons concern goods covered by that emergency under the rules in force that day. Medical devices were being taxed: the industry’s October submission refers to revenue “collected from reciprocal tariffs on medtech since April 2025” [3]. Medicines were exempt: “pharmaceuticals” [4].

points.title: Ending these taxes removes a threat to safe treatment and infection control.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Ending these taxes removes a threat to safe treatment and infection control.

  • Because Hospitals use imported essentials: “These imports include many low-margin, high-use essentials in hospital settings necessary for patient care.” [5]
  • Because Replacing suppliers takes time: “Manufacturers cannot easily pivot to new suppliers, absent multi-year lead times” [3].
  • Because Taxes can make supplies harder to obtain: “Tariffs also may force hospitals to seek new vendors — often at higher cost or with lower reliability.” [5]
  • Because Missing devices threaten patients: “Disruption in the availability of these devices would curtail hospitals’ ability to perform life-saving surgeries and keep patients safe from contagion” [5].
  • So Removing this added burden helps keep supplies available for surgery and infection control when [NAME] needs care.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: AdvaMed says tariffs that cannot be absorbed would likely lead to supply disruptions, and that production of simple items like exam gloves and face masks is moving to Mexico, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic and Malaysia. Sources: [3].

points.title: Lower medical costs help people get needed care.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Lower medical costs help people get needed care.

  • Because Higher hospital costs can reach patients through insurance charges and bills: “This would result in downstream cost shifting to patients through increased premiums, deductibles, and other out-of-pocket expenses.” [6]
  • Because Cost already blocks care; the same article reports people “delaying or skipping care due to cost.” [6]
  • So Removing these taxes eases pressure on medical bills and insurance costs, helping [NAME] obtain care that protects their health.
points.con_html:
Response Lower hospital supply costs do not establish the lower patient charges on which this care-access argument depends. This response does not settle what happens when contracts and premiums are reset.

  • Because The sentence about higher patient charges follows a conditional step: “In the near term, financial pressures could incentivize hospitals to seek higher reimbursement rates from insurers.” [6]
  • Because The hospital association’s October 17 letter explains who bears costs under existing payment rules: “Given that hospital payments are set by government and private payer contracts, the costs would be borne by hospitals directly.” [7]
  • So A tax saving does not itself change an agreed payment rate. The PRO does not establish how savings would reach patients through lower bills, premiums, or deductibles and improve access to care.

points.title: Lower supply costs help hospitals and ambulance services keep staff, services, and reliable equipment.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Lower supply costs help hospitals and ambulance services keep staff, services, and reliable equipment.

  • Because Supply costs compete with care budgets: “Rising supply costs force budget reallocation, limiting investment in staff, technology, and patient care.” [8]
  • Because The hospital association cites a survey, taken in January before the April emergency, in which administrators expected to “delay equipment upgrades to manage financial strain.” [5]
  • Because Equipment quality matters for diagnosis. One surveyed administrator explains: “We do not want to misdiagnose a patient because we have decided to use lower quality equipment that cannot detect their issue.” [8]
  • Because Ambulance services also depend on imports. In April, their association warned about imported supplies and medicines, of which medicines were exempt: “Tariffs on any of these items will increase prices, and could result in product shortages, additional supply chain complexity, and other challenges that EMS simply cannot afford.” [9] EMS means emergency medical services.
  • So Removing taxes on covered supplies eases pressure to cut staff, services, or equipment spending. That protects [NAME]’s access to emergency help and accurate diagnosis.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The NAEMT letter dates from April 2025, cites persistent low EMS reimbursement and asks the Administration to consider EMS impacts of additional tariff actions. Sources: [9].

Evidence note: Becker's reports that the Black Book survey cited in the AHA statement was conducted in late January 2025, before the April emergency, and that it covered tariffs on Chinese imports including pharmaceutical cost expectations. Sources: [10].

points.title: Ending these taxes protects research on better ways to prevent and treat disease.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Ending these taxes protects research on better ways to prevent and treat disease.

  • Because Disease research needs imports that a Johns Hopkins report described in April as taxed: “Biomedical labs rely heavily on imported equipment and materials, from microscopes to diagnostic tools, much of which is now subject to steep tariffs.” [11]
  • Because Higher supply costs threaten that work: “Without affordable access to essential supplies, he warns, American biomedical research could slow down” [11].
  • Because Medical device makers also face pressure on research and development, meaning work on new or better products: “U.S. companies have been shifting resources to manage tariff costs, with R&D spending expected to be the most heavily impacted.” [3]
  • Because That research serves patients. The industry describes its focus as “patient-centered diagnostics and treatments” [3]—ways to find and treat illness.
  • So Removing these costs protects the research that better tests and treatments depend on, advancing [NAME]’s goal of avoiding and overcoming disease.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: HTSUS 9810.00.60 gives duty-free treatment to approved scientific instruments for nonprofit educational or scientific institutions, and August customs guidance excludes Chapter 98 entries from the additional duties, with exceptions. Sources: [12], [13].

points.title: Lower food costs help protect a diet that prevents disease.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Lower food costs help protect a diet that prevents disease.

  • Because Nutritious imports remained taxed in late October. An October 24 report confirmed that major banana suppliers remained covered; an economist explained that “we absolutely should expect a 10% tax on banana imports to drive banana prices higher” [14].
  • Because Higher prices can worsen diets: “During periods of rising prices or uncertainty, households often shift from perishable nutritious foods towards cheaper, longer lasting processed items, reducing the overall quality of the diet.” [15]
  • Because The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) explains why fruits and vegetables matter: “they contribute important nutrients, can reduce the risk for many chronic diseases, and can also help with weight management.” [16]
  • So Ending these taxes lowers a barrier to nutritious food, helping [NAME] protect their health.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: CNBC reports bananas up 5.4% since April, without measuring consumption. The BMJ commentary says tariffs may raise both healthy and unhealthy food costs and fall most on lower-income households. Sources: [14], [15].

points.title: Reducing pressure for layoffs protects workers’ health.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 Reducing pressure for layoffs protects workers’ health.

  • Because Businesses absorbing higher import costs face options including “reduce headcount to offset costs or close shop and go out of business.” [17]
  • Because Job threats affect health: “uncertainty and feelings of job insecurity can harm workers’ mental health, performance, and productivity at work.” [18]
  • So Ending these added costs reduces pressure on employers to cut jobs and the related threat to health, an ordinary risk [NAME] has reason to avoid.

points.title: Lower costs for everyday goods leave more money for medicine and care.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 Lower costs for everyday goods leave more money for medicine and care.

  • Because Higher import costs reach household budgets: “Most of these costs are likely to be passed along to American consumers.” [17]
  • Because A survey conducted in October found that some respondents “delayed or skipped buying doctor-prescribed medication in the past year due to their finances” [19].
  • So Removing these added charges leaves more income available for medicine and medical visits, helping [NAME] keep up needed treatment.

points.title: Ending a source of financial stress protects health.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 Ending a source of financial stress protects health.

  • Because A May survey of reactions to tariffs found “most participants reporting emotions like stress, pessimism, frustration, or anxiety.” [20]
  • Because Stress affects health, beyond unpleasant feelings. The CDC lists “Nightmares or problems sleeping” [21] and “Physical reactions, such as headaches, body pains, stomach problems, or skin rashes” [21].
  • So Ending this source of higher prices removes a cause of financial worry and its health risks, serving [NAME]’s concern for health.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Reach3 result is a press release on consumer sentiment with a combined category of negative emotions. CDC lists possible effects of stress in general. Sources: [20], [21].

points.title: More affordable alarms and fire alerts help protect homes.
points.pro_html:
Point 9 More affordable alarms and fire alerts help protect homes.

  • Because The Security Industry Association warned in April that global tariffs “will directly increase the cost of essential security and life safety products” [22].
  • Because These products protect households: “Consumers need access to alarm and camera systems and fire prevention and alert devices to keep their homes safe.” [22]
  • So Removing taxes on covered safety products lowers a barrier to protection against intrusion and fire, helping [NAME] stay personally safe.

points.title: Lower costs for water treatment help protect safe drinking water.
points.pro_html:
Point 10 Lower costs for water treatment help protect safe drinking water.

  • Because Reporting on the April 2 tariffs explains the risk to imported treatment equipment: “If the new tariffs drive up costs, or cause supply shortages, water utilities may face delays in maintenance and critical infrastructure projects.” [23]
  • Because Treatment protects health: “Drinking water utilities clean (treat) water to remove harmful germs and chemicals and meet safety standards.” [24]
  • So Removing taxes on covered equipment helps utilities fund the treatment and maintenance that protect [NAME] from contaminated drinking water.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: In August 2025, 407 product codes were added to Section 232 metals duties. For those goods, the metal content falls under Section 232 and the rest remains subject to reciprocal tariffs. Sources: [25], [26].

points.title: More affordable helmets help prevent cycling injuries.
points.pro_html:
Point 11 More affordable helmets help prevent cycling injuries.

  • Because In May, with much higher rates then applying to China, PeopleForBikes warned that current and proposed helmet tariffs make protection “much less affordable, which could leave both adults and children unprotected from potential injury.” [27]
  • So Removing these added taxes lowers a barrier to wearing protection during an ordinary activity, serving [NAME]’s wish to avoid injury.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The helmet letter was reported in May when China faced tariffs of 145%. By the bill date the higher rate was suspended, a 10% reciprocal rate remained, and other U.S. tariffs on China remained. Sources: [27], [28].

points.title: Lower costs for workplace safety gear help prevent injuries.
points.pro_html:
Point 12 Lower costs for workplace safety gear help prevent injuries.

  • Because A safety equipment industry report on tariffs enacted on and after April 2 warns about personal protective equipment, or PPE: “the current tariffs will drive up PPE costs across the board, leaving companies with few options: raise prices, cut labor, or reduce their investment in safety equipment.” [29]
  • Because Cutting protection threatens personal safety; the report warns of “preventable injuries and fatalities” [29].
  • So Ending these taxes removes pressure to cut workplace protection, reducing an injury risk [NAME] has reason to avoid.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: ISEA's study covers tariffs enacted on and after April 2, 2025, and an Inc. report on it describes purchasing cuts without splitting tariffs by legal authority. Sources: [29], [30].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose S.J.Res.88?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect If it took effect on October 30, 2025, S.J.Res.88 would end the April 2 tariff emergency and the extra import taxes based on it, at their October 30 rates. The emergency “is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [1] Ending it also removes the power to adjust those taxes under that declaration: “any powers or authorities exercised by reason of said emergency shall cease to be exercised after such specified date” [31].

points.title: It removes support for U.S. medical-supply factories that provide a backup during health emergencies.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It removes support for U.S. medical-supply factories that provide a backup during health emergencies.

  • Because These taxes cover medical gloves from suppliers beyond China. For rubber surgical gloves, an October 9 analysis records a “19% tariff on those from Malaysia” [32]. The October 26 Malaysia agreement keeps “at 19 percent the reciprocal tariffs first set forth in Executive Order 14257 of April 2, 2025” [33].
  • Because U.S. medical-supply makers explain the link to emergency production: “Reciprocal tariffs aren’t just about fairness; they’re about ensuring that our nation can produce life-saving medical supplies when they matter most.” [34]
  • Because Reliable supplies protect patients and the public. The U.S. health department says protective gear and medical equipment “serve vital roles in protecting patients, healthcare workers, and the public.” [35] It also identifies the need to keep domestic suppliers in business: “the U.S. Government has a vested interest in U.S. companies' continued marketplace viability” [35].
  • So Ending the tax removes a price advantage for domestic gloves and support for keeping that capacity available during disruptions to overseas supplies.
  • So [NAME] needs infection protection and safe medical care. Preserving that supply backup gives [NAME] a personal health reason to oppose the bill.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO's price advantage does not establish that these emergency taxes keep medical backup production available. This response does not deny that the tax gives domestic gloves some price advantage over Malaysian gloves.

  • Because A U.S. glove maker's restart was linked to taxes on China: “new U.S. tariffs on rubber gloves from China have doubled the price from a few months ago” [36]; “SafeSource restarted two production lines to accommodate recent new orders” [36].
  • Because The bill targets “the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025” [1]. China’s separate glove duties come from a different trade law: the U.S. trade office decided to “increase the rate of additional duties on medical gloves to 50 percent in 2025” [37].
  • Because After the restart, SafeSource announced in August that it was “suspending activity immediately at its nitrile glove and man-made fiber PPE plants because of poor market conditions” [38]. Its president said those conditions “do not permit sustained domestic production.” [38]
  • So Production did not last at that maker with the emergency taxes in place. The Malaysian import tax and statements supporting U.S. factories do not establish an available medical backup that the bill would put at risk.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The July article on SafeSource says the firm's imported nitrile chemicals became subject to the 10% base tariff. SafeSource suspended its U.S. glove and PPE plants on August 22, 2025, putting 541 employees out of work, and cited market conditions unsupportive for several years. Sources: [36], [38].

Evidence note: Autor, Beck, Dorn and Hanson report that the 2018-2019 import tariffs did not appear to increase manufacturing employment. Flaaen and Pierce report that U.S. manufacturing industries more exposed to tariff increases had relative employment reductions, with a positive protection effect offset by input costs and retaliation. Both studies concern earlier tariffs. Sources: [39], [40].
