directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.J.Res.88?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect If it took effect on October 30, 2025, the resolution would end the April 2 emergency and stop charging its added taxes on new imports. The emergency “is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [1] Federal law requires that “any powers or authorities exercised by reason of said emergency shall cease to be exercised after such specified date” [2]. The reasons below concern imports still covered on that date. Customs applies these taxes to goods “other than those that fall within the identified exceptions” [3].

points.title: It cuts costs that weaken military suppliers and military buying power.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It cuts costs that weaken military suppliers and military buying power.

  • Because Military supply chains use imported parts. Senator Shaheen identified sectors that “source a large part of their components from outside North America” [4].
  • Because The defense import-tax exemption leaves out shared military and commercial stock when tracking the two separately is too costly or impractical. Its exclusions cover supplies “identical in nature to supplies purchased by the Contractor or any subcontractor in connection with its commercial business” [5] when “It is not economical or feasible to account for such supplies so as to ensure that the amount of the supplies for which duty-free entry is claimed does not exceed the amount purchased in connection with this contract.” [5]
  • Because Costs absorbed by suppliers threaten the firms and workers that make military equipment. Shaheen warned in April that this “could drive more companies and jobs out of the defense industrial supply chain, stifling innovation.” [4]
  • Because When suppliers pass higher costs to the military, the same budget buys less. The Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) explains: “As a result, the Department of Defense simply cannot buy as much with its budget.” [6]
  • So Ending these taxes on covered stock outside the defense exemption removes a cost from military production.
  • So Protecting suppliers and military buying power strengthens the state's ability to equip its forces and defend its citizens.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: An October 6, 2025 legal report says a Pentagon memorandum clarified that the DFARS Duty-Free Entry clause applies to tariffs as well as duties, and that contractors failing to use it could absorb those costs. The clause excludes some commingled commercial stock. Sources: [7], [5].

points.title: It removes a barrier to joint defense with allies and partners.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It removes a barrier to joint defense with allies and partners.

  • Because The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) identifies tariffs on Australia as a threat to alliance trust: they have “the potential to significantly erode trust in the U.S.-Australia alliance.” [8]
  • Because Trade friction also limits closer defense ties with New Zealand. CSIS reports that it is “shrinking the permission space for New Zealand leaders to align more closely with the United States on key policy issues, such as potentially joining AUKUS Pillar II.” [8]
  • Because AUKUS is a U.S. defense partnership with Australia and the United Kingdom. The 2022 U.S. security strategy explains its purpose: “Our AUKUS security partnership with Australia and the United Kingdom promotes stability in the Indo-Pacific while deepening defense and technology integration.” [9]
  • Because The damage also obstructs joint action on China's trade practices. Brookings concludes: “This means a coalition focused on addressing the trade challenges with China cannot be built while the United States treats its allies as economic rivals.” [10]
  • So Ending these taxes removes a source of distrust and political resistance to cooperation. That helps the United States work with partners on shared defense and economic threats.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Commerce Secretary Lutnick said in 2025 that if the tariff power were taken away the President had other authorities: "we just bring on another or another or another." Treasury Secretary Bessent said in September there were other authorities "not as efficient, not as powerful." Sources: [11], [12].

Evidence note: CSIS reports public support for the U.S.-Australia alliance remains high despite tariffs, and recommends greater consistency in U.S. policy. Sources: [8].

points.title: It lowers the cost of keeping supply options outside China.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It lowers the cost of keeping supply options outside China.

  • Because U.S. firms have moved production beyond China to protect supplies. CSIS describes an effort to “diversify manufacturing supply chains and protect from shocks that were made apparent during the Covid-19 pandemic and from export controls, sanctions, and other punitive economic measures targeting China.” [13]
  • Because These taxes reach the alternative production sites. Brookings reports: “Southeast Asian countries like Vietnam, Thailand, and Cambodia—popular destinations for Taiwanese manufacturers as they diversify their supply chains away from China—face U.S. tariff rates similar to Taiwan’s, making diversification to Southeast Asia less cost-effective.” [10]
  • So Ending these taxes lowers the cost of importing covered goods from those alternative suppliers. Cheaper supply options make it easier to maintain backups against disruptions and foreign pressure, strengthening U.S. resilience.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO treats production outside China as evidence of supply routes protected from Chinese pressure. This response concerns the electronics evidence below and does not deny that some alternatives exist.

  • Because Brookings' cost comparison concerns manufacturing locations: “Southeast Asian countries like Vietnam, Thailand, and Cambodia—popular destinations for Taiwanese manufacturers as they diversify their supply chains away from China—face U.S. tariff rates similar to Taiwan’s, making diversification to Southeast Asia less cost-effective.” [10] That comparison does not establish whether those factories can supply goods during a Chinese disruption.
  • Because Rhodium Group's review of electronics finds that “these emerging production hubs still rely heavily on Chinese components” [14], while “a range of countries like Malaysia and Singapore are also emerging as specialized component producers” [14]. A factory outside China can still depend on parts from China.
  • Because Rhodium identifies the resulting exposure: “It also gives the Chinese government leverage over the pace and extent of de-risking” [14]. In plain words, China can still influence efforts to reduce dependence on it.
  • So A cheaper place to assemble goods does not by itself establish protection against pressure on their Chinese inputs.

points.title: It reduces pressure on essential water systems.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It reduces pressure on essential water systems.

  • Because Water utilities rely on foreign equipment: “U.S. water systems are deeply reliant on imported gear” [15].
  • Because Higher import costs squeeze utility budgets. WaterWorld's analysis of the April 2 order states: “The tariffs will make importing these items more expensive for utilities. These increased costs could translate into higher utility rates and budget constraints.” [16]
  • Because Those costs threaten maintenance: “If the new tariffs drive up costs, or cause supply shortages, water utilities may face delays in maintenance and critical infrastructure projects.” [16]
  • Because Water services protect the public from disease. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) states: “Safe drinking water is a prerequisite for protecting public health and all human activity, and properly treated wastewater is vital for preventing disease and protecting the environment.” [17]
  • Because Emergency response also depends on water. The same plan lists “Firefighting and hazardous material spill and event responses” [17] among emergency services that need drinking water supplies.
  • So Ending these taxes on covered treatment equipment removes a cost obstacle to timely repairs and upgrades.
  • So Keeping water and sewage systems working protects the public from disease and supports emergency response, strengthening the country's ability to protect its citizens.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Water Daily's April article says "No federal carve-outs so far," while Customs guidance excludes some Canadian and Mexican goods. An October water-equipment warning concerns Section 232 metals duties, which the bill leaves in place. Sources: [15], [3], [18].

points.title: It protects medical supplies needed for surgery and infection control.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It protects medical supplies needed for surgery and infection control.

  • Because Hospitals depend on foreign supplies: “international sources supply a significant proportion of essential medical goods.” [19]
  • Because These include devices that prevent infection: “Some of these devices are single-use, designed to protect patients from infection, such as single-use blood pressure cuffs, stethoscope covers and sterile drapes.” [19]
  • Because The American Hospital Association warns that tariffs “may force hospitals to seek new vendors — often at higher cost or with lower reliability.” [19]
  • Because Supply disruptions “would curtail hospitals’ ability to perform life-saving surgeries and keep patients safe from contagion” [19].
  • Because Higher costs also threaten the continued provision of care: “Persistent expense growth threatens hospitals’ solvency and ability to sustain comprehensive services in their communities.” [19]
  • So Ending these taxes on covered medical devices removes a cost and supply risk from hospitals. It helps preserve the country's ability to protect people from serious illness and infection.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Becker's reports that the Black Book survey cited in the AHA statement was conducted in late January 2025, before the April emergency, and that it covered tariffs on Chinese imports including pharmaceutical cost expectations. Sources: [20].

points.title: It eases economic strain across the country.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It eases economic strain across the country.

  • Because The Chamber of Commerce reports: “Small businesses, manufacturers, and ranchers are struggling with higher costs, with additional economic pain likely in the coming months.” [21]
  • Because Federal Reserve researchers explain that “rising global tariffs dampen economic growth by disrupting trade flows, misallocating resources, and increasing input costs for businesses and goods prices for consumers” [22].
  • Because Economic strength supports national security and social cohesion. The 2022 U.S. security strategy calls the middle class “critical to our national security as an engine of economic growth and a key source of democratic vibrance and cohesion.” [9]
  • So Removing these taxes eases costs and trade disruption for U.S. firms and households. Reducing that nationwide strain supports the economic base of a strong, stable country.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO moves from evidence about prices and growth to a claim about national protection and social stability without establishing that step.

  • Because The Chamber reports that businesses “are struggling with higher costs” [21]. Federal Reserve researchers describe how tariffs “dampen economic growth by disrupting trade flows, misallocating resources, and increasing input costs for businesses and goods prices for consumers” [22]. These statements concern costs and economic activity.
  • Because The security strategy calls the middle class “critical to our national security as an engine of economic growth and a key source of democratic vibrance and cohesion.” [9] It does not establish that the particular costs removed here threaten that cohesion or the country's ability to protect its citizens.
  • So An economic gain and a reduction in threats to national stability are different outcomes. The PRO's general statement about the middle class does not establish the security effect of this particular tax change.

points.title: It removes a source of uncertainty that holds back investment.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 It removes a source of uncertainty that holds back investment.

  • Because The emergency lets the President raise these taxes by changing the import-tax rate list (HTSUS). The order says: “Should any trading partner retaliate against the United States in response to this action through import duties on U.S. exports or other measures, I may further modify the HTSUS to increase or expand in scope the duties imposed under this order to ensure the efficacy of this action.” [23]
  • Because Uncertainty has its own cost. Federal Reserve researchers explain that “trade policy uncertainty, including around tariffs, likely causes firms to delay investment, potentially slowing economic activity even without any actual tariff changes” [22].
  • Because Production capacity is needed for defense. CFR explains: “the United States needs people, materials, and production capacity to field military forces.” [6]
  • So Ending the emergency ends the power to change rates under it. Removing that source of uncertainty helps firms plan investments in the production capacity the country needs to remain strong and withstand shocks.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO equates ending rate changes under one order with reducing the policy uncertainty that delays investment. This response does not deny that this order's own power to change rates would end.

  • Because The bill ends the emergency “declared on April 2, 2025, by the President in Executive Order 14257” [1]. Its text does not end other tariff powers.
  • Because Lutnick had announced replacement action if the emergency tariff power were blocked: “we just bring on another or another or another.” [11] In September, Treasury Secretary Bessent again said, “And there are lots of other authorities that can be used - not as efficient, not as powerful,” [12]. The stated intent to replace blocked tariffs gives firms a concrete policy to consider.
  • Because The Federal Reserve's finding concerns firms' response to “trade policy uncertainty, including around tariffs” [22]. Firms planning investment must consider the announced policy of replacement as well as the fate of this one order.
  • So Repeal would leave firms facing decisions about replacement tariffs and their rates. The PRO has not shown that ending this legal route would ease the uncertainty holding back the production investment it invokes.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Commerce Secretary Lutnick said in 2025 that if the tariff power were taken away the President had other authorities: "we just bring on another or another or another." Treasury Secretary Bessent said in September there were other authorities "not as efficient, not as powerful." Sources: [11], [12].

points.title: It removes a source of shocks to U.S. financial markets.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 It removes a source of shocks to U.S. financial markets.

  • Because Federal Reserve researchers traced a concrete disruption to news about these taxes: “On the morning of Monday, April 7th, a rumored tariff pause and its swift rebuttal within minutes triggered significant intraday volatility in US Treasury yields and precipitated a sharp decline in liquidity across US Treasury cash and futures markets.” [24]
  • Because Liquidity means the ease of buying and selling an asset. The Federal Reserve explains the danger: “In extreme cases, low liquidity can threaten continued market functioning, leading to a situation in which participants are unable to trade without incurring a significant cost.” [25]
  • Because This concerns a core part of U.S. finance: “Treasury market liquidity is particularly important because of the key role these securities play in the financial system.” [25]
  • So Ending this tariff program removes a source of sudden policy news that has strained trading in U.S. government debt. Reducing that risk supports the country's financial stability.
points.con_html:
Response Ending this emergency does not establish an end to sudden news about the administration's tariff policy. This response does not deny the April shock or that this order's own rate changes would end.

  • Because The announced response to losing the tariff power was to “bring on another or another or another.” [11]
  • So Sudden tariff news could continue under other powers. The PRO needs a reason to expect less of it after repeal; the April shock does not supply one.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Commerce Secretary Lutnick said in 2025 that if the tariff power were taken away the President had other authorities: "we just bring on another or another or another." Treasury Secretary Bessent said in September there were other authorities "not as efficient, not as powerful." Sources: [11], [12].

Evidence note: The Federal Reserve note compares April 2025 Treasury market stress with "much-improved market conditions in September 2025." It does not estimate the effect of ending this emergency. Sources: [24].

points.title: It uses a legal safeguard against unchecked emergency rule.
points.pro_html:
Point 9 It uses a legal safeguard against unchecked emergency rule.

  • Because The emergency concerns an enduring trade pattern: “large and persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficits” [23].
  • Because The Brennan Center explains the limit on emergency rule: “Emergency powers are not meant to solve long-standing problems, no matter how serious those problems may be. Nor are they intended to give a president the ability to bypass Congress and act as an all-powerful policymaker.” [26]
  • Because Congress has a lawful way to end this use of power. An emergency ends when “there is enacted into law a joint resolution terminating the emergency” [2].
  • Because Divided powers help protect the country. The 2017 U.S. security strategy describes “separating Federal powers, and protecting the rights of individuals through the rule of law.” [27] It adds: “We protect American sovereignty by defending these institutions, traditions, and principles” [27].
  • So Enacting the resolution applies Congress's legal check to this emergency. Keeping executive power subject to standing rules protects dependable self-government, supporting the secure and stable state [NAME] values.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO's premise that a long-running problem cannot support this emergency is a contested reading of the law. This response does not deny that the resolution applies Congress's check.

  • Because The emergency law permits action against “any unusual and extraordinary threat, which has its source in whole or substantial part outside the United States” [28]. Its text does not say that a threat must be sudden or unforeseen. The age of the trade problem alone does not establish failure of that legal test.
  • Because The 2017 strategy's statement about “separating Federal powers, and protecting the rights of individuals through the rule of law.” [27] supports those safeguards in general. It does not establish that continuing this declaration would defeat them or threaten national stability.
  • So A lawful power to end an emergency, combined with a general defense of constitutional safeguards, does not establish the misuse the PRO relies on or a security benefit from ending this one.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: A November 2025 letter from senators says multiple courts found these tariffs exceed IEEPA, and an October analysis says the Court of International Trade and Federal Circuit ruled against them; the Supreme Court had the case on the bill date. The statutory standard is "unusual and extraordinary threat." Sources: [29], [30], [28].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose S.J.Res.88?
directions.main_effect_html:
Main effect If enacted on October 30, 2025, the bill would end the April 2 emergency that day: “is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [1] Ending that emergency means “the corresponding tariffs could not be applied.” [31] These are the extra taxes on imports imposed under that emergency.

  • Because The September 5 order describes exchanging tariff relief for security promises: “I later temporarily suspended the individual ad valorem rate of duty for certain trading partners to reflect the fact that some trading partners had signaled a willingness to undertake meaningful economic and national security commitments with the United States” [32].
  • Because The October 26 Malaysia statement shows this bargain was still being completed: “In the coming weeks, the United States and Malaysia will undertake domestic formalities in advance of the Agreement entering into force.” [33]
  • So Ending these taxes also gives up a bargaining tool: offering cuts in them in return for security commitments.

points.title: The bill removes an extra incentive to make batteries needed by the U.S. military.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill removes an extra incentive to make batteries needed by the U.S. military.

  • Because These taxes cover battery packs. In a September 10 ruling on a Chinese lithium-ion pack, Customs applied an “additional ad valorem rate of duty of 10 percent” [34].
  • Because Battery tariffs offer a way to shift purchases toward U.S. suppliers. Congress's research service explains: “Such a policy might pivot demand toward domestic producers of batteries and battery parts rather than imported sources” [35].
  • Because These are defense supplies. The Defense Department says: “More and more of our platforms, vehicles, and future capabilities rely on lithium-ion batteries.” [36]
  • Because Building U.S. battery production addresses a current military supply risk. In July 2025, government auditors reported efforts “to reduce reliance on foreign sources that are located primarily in China.” [37]
  • So The bill removes an extra incentive to buy U.S.-made batteries and invest in their production. Keeping that incentive supports the supply base for current and future military equipment. That serves [NAME]'s goal of a state able to defend its citizens.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO jumps from a possible price incentive for battery makers to more secure military supplies. This response does not deny that the tax gives U.S. battery makers some price advantage.

  • Because The congressional report identifies a gap between making finished batteries and making their parts: “Domestic investment in further upstream activities, such as battery cell component manufacturing and active material manufacturing, has not kept pace with investment in further downstream processes.” [35]
  • Because Commercial battery growth also needs a link to military needs. The Defense Innovation Unit explains: “Low-demand signal and complex specifications make it challenging for DoD to leverage current commercial battery technology.” [38] The military buys small amounts and needs batteries built to its requirements.
  • So The PRO has not shown that this extra tax adds U.S. capacity for the cells, materials, or usable batteries needed to reduce military reliance on China. A price incentive alone does not establish that security gain.

points.title: The bill gives up bargaining power to keep sensitive technology from strengthening military adversaries.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill gives up bargaining power to keep sensitive technology from strengthening military adversaries.

  • Because In the trade agreement signed October 26, Malaysia promises to work through its own rules to “align with all unilateral export controls in force by the United States, and ensure that its companies do not backfill or undermine these controls.” [40] These are rules limiting where sensitive goods can be sent.
  • Because Such limits address a military threat. The Commerce Department explains its rules for advanced chips: “BIS imposed these new controls to protect U.S. national security interests by restricting certain exports to China that would advance China's military modernization and surveillance efforts.” [44]
  • So Tariff relief gives the United States something to offer for help stopping companies abroad from supplying restricted buyers. The bill removes that lever. Preserving it helps protect the country against adversaries gaining military technology.

points.title: The bill gives up bargaining power for more secure supplies of defense materials.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill gives up bargaining power for more secure supplies of defense materials.

  • Because Suppliers controlled by adversaries can threaten military production. Government auditors warn: “These suppliers may cut off U.S. access to critical materials” [37].
  • Because Magnets are one military need. Auditors report that the F-35 fighter's main contractor “identified prohibited Chinese magnets in the F-35 supply chain” [37].
  • Because Malaysia's October 26 trade commitments offer another supply route: “Malaysia has committed to ensure no restrictions are imposed on the sale of rare earth magnets to U.S. companies.” [33]
  • Because The commitments also support more production: “Malaysia has committed to the expedient development of its critical minerals and rare earths sectors in partnership with U.S. companies, including granting extended operating licenses to create certainty for businesses to increase production capacity.” [33]
  • Because U.S. tax terms are part of the bargain: it promises to “maintain at 19 percent the reciprocal tariffs” [33] and names products “to receive a zero percent reciprocal tariff rate.” [33]
  • So Ending these taxes gives up a tool for securing and backing access to alternative mineral supplies. Protecting military production against foreign cutoffs gives [NAME] a reason to preserve that tool.

points.title: The bill gives up bargaining power to cut financial support for armed threats.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 The bill gives up bargaining power to cut financial support for armed threats.

  • Because Malaysia's trade agreement promises cooperation under its own laws on U.S. sanctions lists, with the aim of “restricting transactions of its nationals with individuals and entities” [40] on those lists. These restrictions limit financial and business ties.
  • Because Businesses abroad help hide oil sales that fund weapons and armed groups. Treasury describes “creating the illusion of non-sanctionable trade between separate entities.” [48]
  • Because Treasury reports that oil allocated to Iran's armed forces is “underwriting the development of ballistic missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as financing regional terrorist groups.” [48]
  • So The bill removes an extra lever for getting foreign help closing these financing routes. Keeping that lever serves [NAME]'s concern that the United States protect itself against armed threats.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not connect Malaysia's pledge to the oil network it cites. This response concerns that example and does not deny that the pledge could reach other transactions by Malaysian nationals.

  • Because The pledge concerns “restricting transactions of its nationals with individuals and entities” [40] on U.S. lists. Its reach depends on transactions involving Malaysian nationals.
  • Because Treasury locates the cited front companies elsewhere: “These companies are established and operate in China” [48]. It also identifies “Singapore-based Oriental Apple Company PTE Ltd” [48]. Naming those firms does not identify a Malaysian transaction that the pledge would restrict.
  • Because Treasury's reference to Malaysian oil concerns false paperwork: a facilitator “likely provided falsified documents concealing the vessel’s identity and certifying its Iranian oil cargo as Malaysian heavy crude oil.” [48] A false cargo label does not establish involvement by Malaysian nationals.
  • So The oil-network evidence establishes a threat. It does not show a Malaysian restriction on that network that keeping this tariff threat would make more likely.

points.title: The bill gives up bargaining power for help defending vital services against computer attacks.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 The bill gives up bargaining power for help defending vital services against computer attacks.

  • Because Cambodia's October 26 trade agreement pairs U.S. tariff terms with security cooperation. It says: “The United States shall apply a revised reciprocal tariff rate on originating goods of Cambodia as set out in Schedule 2 to Annex I.” [50]
  • Because The same agreement commits Cambodia to “collaborating with the United States to address cybersecurity challenges.” [50] Malaysia's agreement also proposes “exchanging information on threats and best practices” [40].
  • Because Computer attacks threaten national safety during crises. U.S. security agencies warn that Chinese state-backed hackers seek the ability to launch “disruptive or destructive cyberattacks against U.S. critical infrastructure in the event of a major crisis or conflict with the United States.” [51]
  • So Sharing threat warnings and defenses helps protect these systems. Ending tariff leverage gives up a way to press for that help. Protecting vital services during a crisis serves [NAME]'s concern for a secure, stable country.

pages.reference: Read this value as held by a Christian traditionalist in the United States, with the religious right as the cultural reference. Tradition here concerns preserving, observing or passing down identifiable inherited customs, religious practices and ways of life, valued for their continuity with the past. Religious endorsement of a general moral goal alone does not establish that connection.
pages.description: S.J.Res.88 would have ended the national emergency President Trump declared on April 2, 2025, to tax imports from nearly every country. Ending it would have canceled the resulting tariffs: a 10% tax on most imports, with higher rates on goods from certain countries.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor S.J.Res.88?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect If it took effect on October 30, 2025, the bill would end the April 2 emergency and stop the import taxes based on it. That emergency “is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [1] Ending the same emergency means “the corresponding tariffs could not be applied.” [2] All cost relief below concerns future imports covered by those taxes. For China, CBP's guidance kept an added reciprocal tax of 10%: covered goods “will be assessed an additional ad valorem duty rate of 10%.” [3]

points.title: It helps churches keep familiar forms of worship music.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It helps churches keep familiar forms of worship music.

  • Because Tariffs raise the cost of imported instruments: “Now, tariffs are causing a big jump in costs for music stores.” [4]
  • Because Evangelical pastor Kevin DeYoung urges churches to retain an established practice: “But if your church already has an organ my advice is to keep using it.” [5]
  • Because He explains its purpose: “The organ fills in the cracks, provides an underneath sound, and encourages churches to sing louder and freer.” [5]
  • So When churches buy or replace covered imported instruments, the bill removes an added cost of keeping their familiar worship music. Preserving that religious practice serves [NAME]'s value of tradition.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The NPR price report says a large portion of musical instruments come from overseas. The stores it profiles sell or rent band instruments, one of them brass only, and it does not mention organs or churches. DeYoung's 2011 advice concerns a church that already has an organ. Executive Order 14257 covers all articles except listed exceptions; the annex tables are not in the packet. Sources: [4], [5], [6].

points.title: It helps families keep Christian Christmas customs.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It helps families keep Christian Christmas customs.

  • Because A Christmas-tree importer reported higher prices caused by tariffs: “it also had to raise prices by 10% as a result of the tariffs.” [7]
  • Because Focus on the Family describes a recurring custom that uses a Christmas tree: “A family slumber party by the Christmas tree is a tradition our kids love year after year.” [8]
  • Because It connects family celebrations to faith: “When we slow down to celebrate, we are showing our family that our faith matters—and that they matter.” [8]
  • So Removing the added tax on covered Christmas goods cuts an ongoing cost of buying or replacing what these customs use. This helps [NAME] preserve family ways of celebrating Christian faith.

points.title: It supports inherited Christian duties of providing for a family and caring for children.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It supports inherited Christian duties of providing for a family and caring for children.

  • Because On the day of the vote, Senator Wyden described the taxes' household burden: “Americans across our country are shouldering the cost of these tariffs, which are taxes jacking up the price of groceries, electronics, clothes, strollers, and other everyday goods.” [9]
  • Because Southern Baptist teaching assigns a husband the “responsibility to provide for, to protect, and to lead his family” [10] and a wife the duty “to serve as his helper in managing the household and nurturing the next generation.” [10]
  • So Removing this added cost of household necessities helps families meet those duties. For [NAME], supporting this inherited pattern of family life is a reason grounded in tradition to favor the bill.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Kansas City Federal Reserve's September 2025 Beige Book says contacts reported suppliers reluctant to lower prices even when tariff rates fell, causing some stickiness in input costs. Sources: [11].
points.retirement_reason: General household provision is the substantive benefit; the religious quotation does not establish continuation of a particular family custom or organization.

points.title: It lowers an added cost of tools parents use to pass Christian faith to children.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It lowers an added cost of tools parents use to pass Christian faith to children.

  • Because Southern Baptist teaching states the inherited duty: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” [10].
  • Because A maker describes a tool for that teaching: “When you squeeze its hand, the Talking Jesus Doll speaks 10 of Jesus' phrases from the Bible – including the Lord's Prayer and John 3:16.” [12]
  • Because CBS documented the maker's exposure to the earlier, higher tariffs: “With sky-high tariffs in place, he had paused shipments from China, and had containers of goods waiting in limbo overseas.” [13]
  • So Ending the remaining reciprocal tax removes an added cost from these imported teaching aids. Helping parents carry out the religious duty of passing their faith to children directly serves [NAME]'s wish to preserve Christian beliefs across generations.
points.con_html:
Response A seller's claim that a doll teaches Bible verses does not establish that the doll helps [NAME] pass on an accepted Christian tradition.

  • Because The maker states its aim: “The objective of the doll is to make the love and lessons of Jesus tangible for young children.” [12]
  • Because The Southern Baptist teaching calls parents to teach “spiritual and moral values” [10]; it does not identify this product as a way to do so.
  • Because The fit between images of Jesus and inherited Christian teaching cannot be assumed. Defending the Westminster catechism's rule against such images, James Norris writes, “since an image of God cannot be a medium for worship it ought never to be a tool for education in the faith.” [14]
  • So The PRO supplies the maker's purpose, but no basis for placing this aid within the tradition [NAME] seeks to keep. Lower import costs for the doll do not supply that missing link between the product and following [NAME]'s religion.

points.title: It helps families continue regular church offerings and Christmas gospel outreach.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It helps families continue regular church offerings and Christmas gospel outreach.

  • Because Southern Baptist teaching says “Christians should contribute of their means cheerfully, regularly, systematically, proportionately, and liberally for the advancement of the Redeemer’s cause on earth.” [10]
  • Because An April report warned that tariff-driven price rises put giving at risk: “At the same time, donors may give less as they face rising prices and a turbulent stock market.” [15]
  • So Relieving this pressure on household budgets helps protect families' ability to keep regular offerings and fund church work.
  • Because Gift-based outreach is another established practice: “Operation Christmas Child has been collecting and delivering shoebox gifts to children worldwide for more than three decades.” [16]
  • Because Participants pack a “shoebox gift filled with fun toys, school supplies, and personal care items” [16]. These goods include a heavily imported product: “Over 80% of toys sold in the U.S. are made in China, according to The Toy Association trade group.” [13]
  • Because Franklin Graham states the religious purpose: “these simple gifts open the door for the Gospel.” [16]
  • So Removing the added tax on commercially imported toys bought for these gifts lowers a cost of continuing this outreach. Regular church offerings and this established Christmas gospel practice are the traditions at stake.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The Kansas City Federal Reserve's September 2025 Beige Book says contacts reported suppliers reluctant to lower prices even when tariff rates fell, causing some stickiness in input costs. Sources: [11].

Evidence note: The charity report is from April 2025 and names food and clothing among nonprofit costs. The Toy Association figure covers all U.S. toy sales, not shoebox items. Sources: [15], [13].

points.title: It upholds the inherited constitutional order defended within the religious right.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It upholds the inherited constitutional order defended within the religious right.

  • Because The bill lets Congress check presidential tariff policy. Senator Murkowski called the vote “Congress reasserting our authority as a co-equal branch of government with defined powers and responsibilities.” [17]
  • Because Family Research Council treats respect for that inherited order as a conservative commitment: “The written Constitution was designed to permanently explain what the federal government was to be, what it could do, and what it could not do.” [18]
  • Because A 2017 Family Research Council brief on a judicial nominee, mainly concerned with judicial power, also names elected lawmaking and the executive's adherence to law: “The primacy of law-making by our elected representatives and the adherence to the rule of law by the executive branch form the keystone of our governmental framework.” [19]
  • So Ending this presidential emergency through Congress puts those established commitments into practice. [NAME]'s wish to maintain traditional ways of thinking gives that use of Congress's power weight in favor of the bill.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The NEA provides for a vote "to determine whether that emergency shall be terminated." The FRC brief cited by the PRO is a 2017 document supporting a judicial nominee and goes on to discuss the growth of judicial power. The Administration argues Congress delegated this authority under IEEPA. Sources: [20], [19], [21].
points.retirement_reason: Constitutional checks and a conservative organization's approval do not establish preservation or observance of an inherited cultural or religious practice.

points.title: It puts an older Christian teaching about justice in trade into practice.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 It puts an older Christian teaching about justice in trade into practice.

  • Because American Calvinist Frederick Nymeyer's 1956 critique applied inherited religious standards to tariffs: “Nymeyer argued that tariffs violate well-established biblical principles of justice and honesty.” [22]
  • Because Acton Institute carried that teaching forward in 2016: “Christians should reject protectionist tariffs not only because they are economically unsound, but also because of their immorality and incompatibility with Christianity.” [23]
  • Because These taxes seek to encourage home production through higher import costs. The White House says the remaining reciprocal tax is meant “to encourage domestic production” [24].
  • Because The consumer burden criticized in that tradition applies here. Senator Paul explained the taxes targeted by the resolution: “They drive up the costs for things Americans buy every day and make it harder for American businesses to thrive and create more jobs” [9].
  • So Ending these import taxes follows this strand of Christian teaching about biblical justice in trade. Honoring that teaching gives [NAME] a reason grounded in tradition to favor the bill.
points.con_html:
Response The age and Christian authorship of the arguments against import taxes do not establish them as teachings [NAME] has a reason from tradition to follow.

  • Because Christianity Today describes Nymeyer as “A protégé of libertarian economist Ludwig von Mises and a Calvinist himself” [22]. The article presents his application of biblical principles to a disputed policy.
  • Because Acton's conclusion is the author's policy judgment: “Christians should reject protectionist tariffs not only because they are economically unsound, but also because of their immorality and incompatibility with Christianity.” [23]
  • Because The American Family Association offers a different account of the religious rule: “Tariffs are not inherently good or evil. They are tools – sometimes necessary, often risky, and always consequential.” [25]
  • So The PRO must connect the particular Nymeyer–Acton reading to the religious or cultural teaching [NAME] seeks to maintain. Showing that two Christian writers made the argument decades apart does not establish that connection. Applying an old biblical principle to trade is not, by itself, evidence that the policy judgment is an inherited teaching for [NAME].
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Christianity Today presents Nymeyer as a Calvinist businessman, protégé of Mises, in a dispute with Kuyper's different view. American Family Association's The Stand says tariffs are not inherently good or evil. Sources: [22], [25].
points.retirement_reason: The justification is justice and honest dealing. Calling a tariff position biblical does not supply a distinct Tradition connection.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose S.J.Res.88?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect If enacted on October 30, 2025, the bill would end the April 2 emergency and the extra import taxes based on it. The emergency “is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [1] Ending it means “the corresponding tariffs could not be applied.” [2] This removes protection for U.S. makers competing with taxed imports: “by making foreign goods more expensive, tariffs make domestic products more competitive.” [25] American Giant is one maker that produces at home: NPR reports that it “sources and manufactures almost all its products in the U.S., from cotton to the final stitch.” [26]

points.title: Removing protection for factory work puts traditional marriage and family roles at risk.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Removing protection for factory work puts traditional marriage and family roles at risk.

  • Because A U.S. study of growing imports from China during 1990–2014 found harm to men's work and pay: “On average, trade shocks differentially reduce employment and earnings of young adult males.” [27]
  • Because Those earnings losses affect family life: “shocks to males' relative earnings reduce marriage and fertility.” [27]
  • Because Marriage and the husband's provider role are religious commitments in [NAME]'s cultural tradition. The Southern Baptist faith statement says, “Marriage is the uniting of one man and one woman in covenant commitment for a lifetime.” [28] Of a husband, it says, “He has the God-given responsibility to provide for, to protect, and to lead his family.” [28]
  • Because That family pattern also carries a duty to pass on the faith: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” [28].
  • So By removing a defense against import-driven job and pay losses, the bill puts marriage and the provider role at greater risk. Keeping those religious roles and passing them on gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.
points.con_html:
Response A price advantage for U.S. products does not establish that these taxes protect the men's jobs and pay on which the family argument depends.

  • Because The bill says the April 2 emergency “is terminated effective on the date of the enactment of this joint resolution.” [1] The relevant comparison is keeping or ending its import taxes as of October 30, 2025.
  • Because The family study ties marriage losses to men's earnings relative to women's: “shocks to males' relative earnings reduce marriage and fertility.” [27] It studies rising Chinese import competition during 1990–2014, not the effects of these taxes.
  • Because A study of local employment under the 2018–2019 taxes reports that “import tariffs do not appear to increase employment in manufacturing” [29]. It directly tests the step from import protection to factory jobs that the marriage study does not test.
  • Because A Federal Reserve study of the 2018–2019 taxes found that “a positive effect from import protection is offset by larger negative effects from rising input costs and retaliatory tariffs.” [30]
  • Because For the 2025 taxes, the textile trade group's president warned in October: “Reciprocal tariffs on these items hurt domestic textile producers and drives offshoring, undermining U.S. manufacturing jobs” [31]. She was discussing taxes on certain imported materials and machinery unavailable at home.
  • So American Giant's U.S. production and a price advantage do not establish that this extra tax layer preserves men's jobs or pay. Without that link, the historical import losses do not establish that ending these taxes puts marriage, husbands' provider roles or passing on the faith at greater risk.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Autor, Beck, Dorn and Hanson report that the 2018-2019 import tariffs did not appear to increase manufacturing employment. Flaaen and Pierce report that U.S. manufacturing industries more exposed to tariff increases had relative employment reductions, with a positive protection effect offset by input costs and retaliation. Both studies concern earlier tariffs. Sources: [29], [30].

points.title: Removing that protection also threatens the local congregations that carry inherited worship customs.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Removing that protection also threatens the local congregations that carry inherited worship customs.

  • Because A study using U.S. church data for 1990–2010 found that Chinese import shocks “led to a reduction in the number of churches” [32]. It also found they “caused an increase in the number of religious adherents” [32].
  • Because Members' means support church life. The Southern Baptist faith statement calls for regular giving: “Christians should contribute of their means cheerfully, regularly, systematically, proportionately, and liberally” [28]. Losing income leaves less money for that duty.
  • Because Losing local work can pull younger generations away from their congregations. The account of the Ragsdale Church of Christ's closure reports, “Young people have left the region seeking employment” [33].
  • Because A congregation is a place where families keep particular customs alive. Ragsdale's final gathering was “an old-time singing — the kind they used to have every fourth Sunday.” [33]
  • Because Worship there was also a family practice across generations. Member Emily Smartt “remembers being there with her parents and late husband.” [33]
  • So Ending this protection puts the jobs and income that help sustain local congregations at risk. Keeping those congregations and their shared customs alive honors [NAME]'s religious heritage, giving [NAME] another reason to oppose the bill.
points.con_html:
Response The church evidence does not show that keeping these taxes protects local congregations or their inherited customs.

  • Because The cited church-study abstract examines “trade shocks to manufacturing industries stemming from Chinese imports” [32], using U.S. church data for 1990–2010. Applying its finding to this bill requires the missing step from point 1: that ending this tax layer harms the jobs or income that support congregations.
  • Because Ragsdale's preacher reported that “Young people have left the region seeking employment” [33]. That example shows a reason members leave; it supplies no link between those departures and the import taxes this bill ends.
  • So Neither source establishes that ending these taxes would cut church income or drive members away. The duty to give and the value of shared worship customs do not fill that gap. The PRO has not shown that the bill threatens the congregations that carry those customs.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: Ragsdale's preacher attributes the congregation's decline to location, societal changes and economics, including generational change. The Cesur et al. abstract finds fewer churches and more adherents following Chinese import shocks in 1990-2010. Sources: [33], [32].
